body:
Can't go in all the details what UE does different but here are a few pointers:

- UE likely has the async or sliced path queries enabled by default, aka uses threads and time slicing for many agents.
- In Godot if you query for a path by default that all happens on the main thread. You can use threads for path queries, the NavigationServer is perfectly thread-safe, but you need to do that deliberately, aka create a `Thread` and call the server from that. For time slicing queries there is no build-in option, you need to do time-slicing in scripting.

- UE has the tile chunk navmesh always enabled by default that bakes navmesh directly from physics geometry. They removed the single-piece navmesh or user input option that is similar to what Godot uses from the user interface a while ago. There is also some hierarchical optimization available due to the tile chunks or world partition actors because it will ignore/unload/hide all the unnessary navmesh chunks automatically to speed up queries with smaller graphs.
- In Godot the navmesh comes from user input and is used as provided by the user. There is no magical partitioning, slicing, chunking or otherwise hierarchical optimization happening behind the scene. You need to do all that manually. If the navmesh is unwieldy big with ten-thousand of polygons those will be used and searched as is. That is also the case in the test project and why it is sooooo slow. Every query needs to search over those 10.000+ polygons because there is nothing that tries to auto-optimize this geometry soup that was the input.

Is performance optimal? No. Can it be improved? Yes. Is it a bug? No. It is a lack of features. Some of the missing features can be solved on the user end (e.g. using threads, optimizing input, chunking navmesh regions) but some can't and would require new features or changes on the server internals (e.g. navmesh auto-slicing, hierarchical graph). 

In general the current performance is what is expected in absence of no additional hand-holding features or auto-optimization behind the scene.

PR https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/102767 adds a limit on how many polygons are max search each query to at least not go performance-ballistic on a giant unoptimized navmesh geometry with thousands of polygons.
PR https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/106670 makes region and links async updatable. Basically the core requirement to later add hierarchical features while not imploding on threads.
PR https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/102766 added filter options so that already region chunked projects can only query navmesh around their current region chunks instead of the entire map.

Other missing features are more involved and while there are plans to add them will take time.

When I made the bug report if of course checked to make sure I am comparing oranges to oranges:
A: I explicitly did not use async queries in Unreal, only the synchronous ones
B: I triple checked that the queries are single threaded in the main game thread

Only after these checks did I file the bug report. Regardless of what the reasoning is, the current implementation is simply way too slow to be usable in production.

I have tested 4.6 Beta 1 and the issue is still present. This simply makes Godot unfeasible choice for any sort of RTS type game.

> Is performance optimal? No. Can it be improved? Yes. Is it a bug? No. It is a lack of features. Some of the missing features can be solved on the user end (e.g. using threads, optimizing input, chunking navmesh regions) but some can't and would require new features or changes on the server internals (e.g. navmesh auto-slicing, hierarchical graph).

Performance being order of magnitude or more worse than what's needed for RTS game of average unit count can be hardly excused as "lack of features".

For example if Godot's renderer Averaged 2-5FPS in a moderately complex level on modern GPUs, instead of 200-500FPS it currently does, I doubt anyone reasonable would describe that as Godot lacking a "feature" of being faster.

Yes, you could also say "User that doesn't need handholding can write their own renderer", but in such case no one would take this engine seriously.
